title: Three Numbers That Add Up to 101%: Rounding Probabilities Without Lying
excerpt: Round the three numbers on a football forecast one at a time and close to a third of rows add up to 99% or 101%. Here is why, the fix that hides problems, the method that doesn't (largest remainder), why a 50 always keeps its decimal, and the rounding traps in JavaScript and Python.
content:
On Sunday 8 November the Vegas Golden Knights play in Buffalo. The market has it at 50% for each side. CrystlQuant's page for the game says Vegas, 50.1%.

That decimal isn't decoration. Everywhere else on the site the numbers are whole: Liverpool 58%, the draw 23%, Crystal Palace 19%. The decimal turns up only here, because without it the page would print 50% and 50% and look like it had refused to answer. A forecast that won't pick a side isn't much of a forecast, so the rule is short: if a number rounds to 50, it keeps a decimal.

I help build CrystlQuant, a free sports forecasting site that posts a win chance for every game before it starts and grades every one afterwards. Printing a probability sounds like the easiest job on the site. It turned out to hide one bug we shipped, one we nearly shipped, and a couple of traps in the rounding functions themselves.

## The row that adds up to 101

A football match has three outcomes: home win, draw, away win. Say the chances are 33.5%, 33.5% and 33.0%. Round each one to a whole number and you get 34, 34 and 33. That's 101%.

```js
const row = [0.335, 0.335, 0.330];
row.map(p => Math.round(p * 100));   // [34, 34, 33]  -> 101
```

No single number is wrong. Each is the correct rounding of a correct value. The bug lives in the row, and it only shows up when somebody adds the row up, which is the first thing a doubtful reader does.

It isn't rare. On the morning of 8 November (Seoul time), CrystlQuant's board had 100 three-way football matches with a forecast. Round each number on its own, from the one-decimal figures, and 30 of those rows print as 99% or 101%: 18 too high, 12 too low. Close to one game in three.

We shipped exactly this in August. The match page rounded its three numbers with three separate calls, and every check on the stored data stayed green, because nothing stored was wrong. The arithmetic only broke on the screen.

## The tempting fix makes things worse

The first idea most people have is to normalise: divide each number by the row's total so the row comes to 100, then round. It doesn't actually solve anything, since the scaled numbers still need rounding and can still land on 99 or 101.

Worse, it hides real problems. If an upstream feed ever sends three probabilities that add up to 108%, a page that forces every row to 100 quietly covers the mistake. A broken row should look broken. So the target isn't a hard-coded 100. It's whatever the inputs add up to, rounded. For a healthy row that's 100; for a broken one it isn't, and the reader can see it.

## Largest remainder

The fix is older than computers. It's the Hamilton method, which the United States once used to share out House seats between states, and the idea fits in three steps:

- Work out the target: the inputs' total, rounded.
- Round every value down.
- Hand out the missing points one at a time, to the values with the biggest fractional parts.

```js
function apportion(probs) {
  const scaled = probs.map(p => p * 100);
  const target = Math.round(scaled.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));
  const out = scaled.map(Math.floor);
  let left = target - out.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const order = scaled
    .map((v, i) => ({ i, frac: v - Math.floor(v) }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.frac - a.frac || a.i - b.i);
  for (let k = 0; left > 0; k++, left--) out[order[k % order.length].i] += 1;
  return out;
}

apportion([0.335, 0.335, 0.330]);   // [34, 33, 33]
```

Here's a real one from the same Sunday. For FC Copenhagen against Brondby, CrystlQuant had 54.7% Copenhagen, 23.6% draw, 21.7% Brondby. Rounded one at a time, that's 55 + 24 + 22 = 101. Largest remainder rounds everything down to 54 + 23 + 21 = 98, then gives the two missing points to the biggest fractions, the two .7s. The page shows 55, 23, 22.

Look at the draw. 23.6 prints as 23. That's the honest cost of the method: one number gets rounded the "wrong" way so the row comes out right. Some rounding error is unavoidable, so you're choosing where it goes, and a row that adds up is the smaller lie.

Two properties make it safe to use on a forecast. First, every value ends up at its own floor or its own ceiling, so the method can make two close numbers look tied but can never print the smaller one above the bigger one. The favourite stays the favourite. Second, ties in the fractions are broken by position in the row (that's the last part of the sort above). It looks fussy, but without it the same game could render two different ways on two reloads, and a number that changes when you press refresh is a number nobody trusts.

## Back to 50

Apportionment and the 50 rule have to work together, in that order. First the row is apportioned to whole numbers. Then any cell that landed on 50 gets one decimal. If one decimal still reads as a tie, say 50.04% against 49.96%, which both print as 50.0, it goes to two decimals, and it stops at three.

A true 50.000% stays 50. That's the one case where the honest answer really is a tie, and with real forecasts it basically never comes up. Everything else gets a side, even if the side is a tenth of a point.

## The rounding functions aren't the ones you learned at school

The last trap is in the tools. Schoolbook rounding sends a half up. The functions you'll actually call often don't:

```js
(1.005).toFixed(2);   // "1.00", not "1.01"
Math.round(-2.5);     // -2
```

```python
round(2.675, 2)                      # 2.67
round(0.5), round(1.5), round(2.5)   # 0, 2, 2
```

1.005 and 2.675 can't be stored exactly in binary floating point. What's stored is a hair under each, so they round down. Python's round uses round-half-to-even, sometimes called banker's rounding, which is why 2.5 goes to 2. JavaScript's Math.round sends a half towards positive infinity, so -2.5 becomes -2.

For a single 58% forecast none of this matters. It matters when two pieces of code round the same number in two slightly different ways. In August we tested two harmless-looking ways of writing one-decimal rounding in JavaScript against every value from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.0001:

```js
Math.round(p * 1000) / 10   // one way
(p * 100).toFixed(1)         // the other
```

They disagreed on 323 of the 10,001 values. Put one on the game page and the other on the board, and the same game shows two different numbers.

So the fix we ended up with is boring on purpose: one rounding function, in one file, and every page calls it. Two pages that each compute the same number correctly but round it differently are still giving two different answers.

## What's left on the screen

All of that machinery ends in something small. A row of three whole numbers that adds up, a favourite that's always shown as the favourite, and a decimal only where a whole number would hide the call.

So when the Golden Knights page says 50.1%, read it for what it is: the smallest call the page can make, and still a call. It's on CrystlQuant's page for the game, crystlquant.com/nhl/game/nhl-2026020278, and after the final horn you'll see it graded there, right or wrong.
